meetings.title: Postmortem: ingest delay
segments: Give it a second, a couple of people are still joining. Tom, you made it.
Just about. I was on the phone with Brightline until two minutes ago.
How did that go?
Tense, but okay. I'll share more when we get to customer impact.
Okay, let's start. Quick reminder that this is a blameless postmortem.
We're here to understand how the system let this happen, not who did what.
Sam, can you walk us through the timeline?
Before we start, can I say thank you to everyone who worked late that day.
I know it was stressful.
Thanks Maya. It was a long afternoon for a few people here.
Sure. At nine twelve in the morning, Eastern, a schema migration started on the events table.
It was adding an index.
It took a lock that blocked writes.
From that point, the ingest workers couldn't write, so everything piled up in the queue.
Who was on call when it started?
I was. But nothing paged me, so I didn't know until Tom's team escalated.
Then it took about twenty minutes to find the blocking lock, because I was looking at the workers first, and they looked healthy.
And that's the system's fault, not yours.
The tools pointed you the wrong way.
Nothing errored. The workers were just waiting.
So none of our alerts fired.
At one forty in the afternoon, Brightline emailed support saying no new feedback had shown up since the morning. That's when we noticed.
Why didn't the worker health checks catch it?
The workers were stuck for hours.
Because they weren't stuck from the health check's point of view.
They were alive, connected, and waiting on a database lock.
The health check only asks 'is the process running', not 'is it making progress'.
That's a subtle one. Alive but not doing anything.
Let's add that as a follow-up.
A progress-based health check, so a worker that hasn't completed a job in some time counts as unhealthy.
I can take the progress-based health check, since I'm already in that code for the lag alert.
Great, thanks Sam. Add it to the doc as yours.
So about four and a half hours before we knew.
Right. We killed the migration at one fifty-two, the lock released, and the queue drained by about three fifteen.
Total delay was around six hours for the worst affected workspaces.
Two hundred and twelve workspaces affected.
We got fourteen tickets and two escalations, one of them Brightline.
What went well?
We didn't lose any data.
The queue held everything, and once the lock released, the workers caught up on their own.
That's the durable queue doing exactly its job.
Was there any risk of losing data if the lock had lasted longer?
Not for a while. The queue retains messages for seven days.
We'd have had to be stuck for a week before anything was at risk.
That was a deliberate decision last year, and it paid off.
Worth writing that down in the postmortem as a thing that worked, so nobody shortens the retention to save money.
And the clustering jobs recovered automatically once the data landed.
What went badly?
Three things. We ran a blocking migration during peak hours.
Our alerting only looks at errors, not at how far behind we are.
And there was no runbook for 'ingest is stuck', so it took a while to find the lock.
Why was the migration run during peak hours?
I'm asking about the process, not the person.
Because we had no rule against it.
The migration looked harmless, adding an index, and our tooling didn't warn that it would lock the table.
The person who ran it followed our process exactly.
The process was the problem.
And to be fair, the same migration on staging took two seconds, because staging has a tiny fraction of the data.
Which is another follow-up. Staging should have realistic data volumes for the big tables, or we should at least test migrations on a copy.
And from the customer side, we had no template for this kind of incident.
My team wrote fourteen slightly different replies.
Brightline got a vague answer first, which didn't help, given they're already unhappy with us.
What should the first message to customers have said?
Something like: we know feedback isn't appearing, nothing is lost, here's when we'll update you next.
Short and honest. Instead, the first reply said we were 'looking into reports of an issue', which sounded like we didn't believe them.
That's fair. We also didn't give support anything to say, because we didn't know ourselves for a while.
Okay. Action items. Let's make them specific and owned.
I'll build a queue lag alert that pages on-call when ingest is more than five minutes behind.
Five minutes feels right. Too low and it pages for normal spikes, too high and we're back to finding out from customers.
I'll evaluate online migration tools, so schema changes don't lock hot tables.
How long would the evaluation take, roughly?
About a week. I want to test at least two tools against a realistic copy of the events table, including one while we're writing to it at peak rates.
A week is fine. Better to pick the right one.
And I'll write a policy.
No blocking schema changes on hot tables during business hours without a review.
Plus a runbook for stuck ingest.
Should the policy cover the ML tables too?
The clustering jobs do big writes at night.
Yes, any table over a certain size.
I'll define the threshold in the policy, probably ten million rows.
And the runbook should include how to find blocking locks.
It took us twenty minutes to find the right query that day.
Agreed. I'll put the exact queries in the runbook.
I'll write an incident communication template for customer-facing incidents, so we respond consistently.
What would the template include?
Three versions. First response within fifteen minutes, saying what we know and when we'll update next.
Regular updates every hour. And a resolution message with a short, honest explanation.
Plus a rule that at-risk accounts get a personal call.
Can engineering get a heads-up before it goes out?
Just so we're telling the same story.
Yes, the on-call engineer reviews the first message.
It takes one minute and avoids contradictions.
One more from me. Brightline should get a personal follow-up, not just the template.
Tom, can you and I call Olivia?
Tom, anything else from customers we should know?
Any requests that came out of this?
Two customers asked for a status page.
And Brightline asked if they could get an alert themselves when their feedback is delayed, instead of noticing on their own.
I'll add both requests to the doc, with the customer names, so we can tell them when it ships.
A customer-facing freshness indicator. That's a good idea, actually.
Let's capture it for the roadmap.
Not now, but it's a nice way to show we take reliability seriously.
Yes, I'll set up a call with Olivia for next week.
Great. I'll write this up and share the postmortem doc.
Thanks everyone, this was really constructive.
